theme: Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 32. David wrote this after the events of the last reading. It is a song of forgiveness, and one of the great teaching psalms in the Bible.
settingTheScene: The title calls it “A Maskil of David,” meaning a song of instruction. It seems to reflect on the period after his sin with Bathsheba, the silence of the months when he hid it, and the relief that came when he confessed. It is one of the seven traditional penitential psalms, but it is characterized more by joy than by sorrow. Placed right after Day 271, it tells the other side of the story.
observation: “Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered” (v. 1).
“Blessed is the man against whom the LORD counts no iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no deceit” (v. 2).
“For when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long” (v. 3).
“For day and night your hand was heavy upon me; my strength was dried up as by the heat of summer” (v. 4).
“I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity; I said, I will confess my transgressions to the LORD, and you forgave the iniquity of my sin” (v. 5).
“You are a hiding place for me; you preserve me from trouble; you surround me with shouts of deliverance” (v. 7).
“I will instruct you and teach you in the way you should go; I will counsel you with my eye upon you” (v. 8).
“Many are the sorrows of the wicked, but steadfast love surrounds the one who trusts in the LORD” (v. 10).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with a double blessing, and uses three words for sin: transgression, sin, and iniquity. Each is matched with a word for forgiveness: forgiven, covered, and not counted. The piling up of terms shows how thoroughly God deals with every type of wrong. He lifts it away, covers it, and does not count it against us.

David then describes the misery of hiding his sin. His body suffered. His bones wasted away. God’s hand was heavy on him. The groaning went on all day. The guilt of unconfessed sin is not just a spiritual problem. It touches the whole person. David knew by experience that silence and concealment do not work. They drain strength like summer heat.

Then comes the turn, in verse 5: “I acknowledged my sin to you.” Notice the three verbs: acknowledged, did not cover, confessed. And the result: “You forgave.” The speed of it is striking. David says he will confess, and God forgives. This is the same forgiveness Nathan announced. God is not reluctant. He is eager to forgive.

The rest of the psalm shows what follows from forgiveness. God becomes a hiding place. The man who ran from God now runs to him. God also becomes a teacher: “I will instruct you.” The forgiven person is ready to learn. And God’s counsel is personal, “with my eye upon you.” The forgiven are guided, not like a mule that needs a bit and bridle, but like a person who follows willingly.

The final verses are an invitation to the whole community: “Be glad in the LORD, and rejoice, O righteous, and shout for joy, all you upright in heart!” Forgiveness leads to joy.
connection: Paul uses verses 1 and 2 in Romans 4:6-8 as proof that God justifies the ungodly by faith, and not by works. “Blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin.” This is the heart of justification: the imputing of righteousness and the non-imputing of sin. Christ became sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). 1 John 1:9 says, “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us.”
application:
If there is any sin you are hiding, confess it today. Do not wait.

Read verses 1 and 2 as a description of your status in Christ.

Ask God to counsel you with his eye upon you. Then listen.
prayerPrompts: Acknowledge your sin to God without covering it.
Thank him for the forgiveness that makes you blessed.
Ask him to be your hiding place.
